sections.summary: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, is led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days of testing by the devil, recapitulating Israel's wilderness experience as the faithful Son who will face the same categories of testing that Israel faced and failed.

The devil challenges Jesus to use his divine sonship for self-provision by turning stone to bread, and Jesus responds with Deuteronomy 8:3, choosing to live by God's word rather than exercising power to meet his own need -- succeeding where Israel grumbled for food in the wilderness.

sections.section_title: The Second Test -- Authority over the Kingdoms
sections.summary: The devil offers Jesus immediate dominion over all kingdoms in exchange for worship, and Jesus responds with Deuteronomy 6:13, refusing the shortcut to political power through idolatrous allegiance -- succeeding where Israel repeatedly turned to the gods of the nations for prosperity and security.

sections.section_title: The Third Test -- The Temple Pinnacle
sections.summary: The devil quotes Psalm 91 to challenge Jesus to throw himself from the temple pinnacle and force God to demonstrate protection, and Jesus responds with Deuteronomy 6:16, refusing to manipulate God through presumption -- succeeding where Israel tested God at Massah by demanding proof of His presence.

The devil departs after exhausting every category of testing, but only temporarily -- 'until an opportune time' (achri kairou) -- signaling that the adversarial testing will return at the Passion (Luke 22:3, 22:53).

Jesus returns to Galilee 'in the power of the Spirit,' begins teaching in synagogues, and is praised by all -- establishing the pattern of Spirit-empowered public ministry and setting up the dramatic reversal that will occur at Nazareth.

sections.section_title: Jesus in the Synagogue at Nazareth -- The Reading
sections.summary: Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1-2a (with an insertion from Isaiah 58:6) in the Nazareth synagogue, defining his Spirit-anointed mission as bringing good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind, freedom to the oppressed, and the proclamation of the favorable year of the Lord, then declares 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
sections.relevance: The mission Jesus announces is defined by categories of human need -- the poor, captives, the blind, the oppressed -- not by a pre-selected group. The Isaiah 61 program, rooted in the Jubilee legislation of Leviticus 25, envisions a comprehensive restoration available to all who are in bondage, debt, or affliction. The deliberate omission of 'the day of vengeance of our God' from Isaiah 61:2 distinguishes the present moment as one of offered favor rather than executed judgment, framing the mission as an open proclamation rather than a selective decree. The public declaration 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' addresses the entire synagogue audience as potential recipients. While the passage is primarily about defining the content and nature of Jesus's mission rather than directly arguing about who determines salvation outcomes, the structure of the proclamation -- universal offer directed at need -- presupposes recipients whose response to the offered favor matters.
key_phrases: to bring good news to the poor
to proclaim release to the captives
to proclaim the favorable year of the Lord
Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing

sections.summary: The synagogue audience initially speaks well of Jesus and marvels at his gracious words but limits their understanding to his local identity ('Is this not Joseph's son?'), and Jesus preemptively addresses their expectation of preferential hometown treatment by declaring that no prophet is welcome in his own hometown.
sections.relevance: The people's response moves from admiration to skepticism based on familiarity, and Jesus identifies this as a pattern of human refusal to receive a prophet. The verbal link between dektos ('welcome/acceptable') in the proverb about the prophet and dektos in the 'favorable year of the Lord' (v. 19) is striking: the year of the Lord's favor is being proclaimed by one whom the hearers choose not to find favorable. The rejection is presented as a human act rooted in assumptions about Jesus's origins, not as a divinely determined outcome. The implication is that the offered favor can be refused by those who assume they already know what God's messenger should look like.
key_phrases: no prophet is welcome in his hometown

sections.summary: Jesus cites two scriptural precedents -- Elijah sent to the Gentile widow of Zarephath during the famine and Elisha healing only Naaman the Syrian among many lepers in Israel -- to argue that God has historically directed saving acts beyond Israel's boundaries when Israel proved unresponsive to the prophet's message.
sections.relevance: This argument directly bears on whether human response affects who receives God's saving action. The logic Jesus presents is that God's saving work goes where it is received: when Israel under Ahab rejected the prophet, God sent Elijah to a Gentile widow; when Israelite lepers did not come to Elisha, God healed a Syrian enemy commander. The neutral reading states the implication explicitly: 'if you reject what God is doing through me, do not assume that God's purposes will therefore fail. God has always had the freedom to go where His message is received, even if that means going outside Israel.' The framework is one in which human rejection is a genuine act that causes God to redirect saving work, and human reception (the widow's hospitality, Naaman's eventual obedience) is a genuine act that results in receiving that saving work. God retains sovereign freedom over where to direct His saving action, but human response is the factor that triggers the redirection.
key_phrases: there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah
Elijah was sent to none of them, but only to Zarephath
there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha
none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian

sections.summary: The synagogue audience is filled with rage at the Elijah-Elisha argument, drives Jesus out of the city, and attempts to throw him off a cliff, but he passes through their midst and goes his way.
sections.relevance: The people's violent rejection confirms the pattern Jesus just described: those who assume privileged access to God's favor are the ones who reject the prophet when the implications of his message become uncomfortable. The neutral reading notes that 'they responded not with repentance but with violence -- thereby confirming the very pattern Jesus described,' which presupposes that repentance was a genuine option they chose not to exercise. The transition from admiration (v. 22) to attempted murder (v. 29) is driven entirely by human choice -- specifically by the refusal to accept that God's saving work is not Israel's exclusive possession. Jesus's sovereign escape ('passing through their midst') shows that human rejection cannot thwart God's plan, but the rejection itself is presented as a genuine human act with real consequences: the saving work announced in Isaiah 61 moves on, away from those who refused it.
key_phrases: all the people in the synagogue were filled with rage
drove Him out of the city
in order to throw Him down the cliff
passing through their midst, He went His way

sections.summary: Jesus moves to Capernaum and teaches on the Sabbath with an authority (exousia) that amazes the people -- an authority that does not derive from citing earlier teachers but is intrinsic to his person.

Jesus exorcises an unclean demon from a man in the Capernaum synagogue, demonstrating in action the 'release to the captives' announced in the Nazareth proclamation, while silencing the demon's accurate identification of him as 'the Holy One of God' because his identity must be revealed through his actions and on his own terms.

Jesus heals Simon's mother-in-law of a high fever by rebuking it with the same authoritative command used against the demon, and she immediately rises and serves them, demonstrating the completeness and immediacy of the restoration.

After the Sabbath ends, Jesus heals many sick individuals by laying hands on each one personally and exorcises demons who identify him as 'the Son of God,' with the author noting editorially that 'they knew Him to be the Christ' -- the first explicit connection of 'Son of God' with 'Christ' in the narrative.

Jesus withdraws to a secluded place, refuses the crowds' attempt to keep him in Capernaum, and declares 'I must (dei) proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also, because I was sent for this purpose' -- introducing the key Lukan theological marker dei (divine necessity) that identifies the events of Jesus's ministry as the unfolding of God's predetermined plan.
